topic: Research: Semantic Kernel & AutoGen to Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0: Migration Guide

key_points: Official Semantic Kernel migration guide maps namespaces, package imports, agent creation, sessions/threads, tools, invocation, streaming, dependency injection, and agent type consolidation.
Core migration theme: replace Kernel-centered agent construction with Agent Framework agents built on Microsoft.Extensions.AI/.NET or agent_framework Python chat clients.

Strong writer takeaway: existing KernelFunction and VectorStore investments do not need to be thrown away; compatibility helpers can convert Semantic Kernel functions and vector search into Agent Framework tools.

Official AutoGen migration guide covers model clients, single-agent feature mapping, tools, hosted tools, MCP, agent-as-tool patterns, middleware, custom agents, group chat replacements, human-in-the-loop, checkpointing, and observability.
Frames Agent Framework as the new foundation developed by core AutoGen and Semantic Kernel teams, with side-by-side migration examples for Python developers.
Best section to emulate: divide the article into what stays familiar, what changes, and how to validate each migrated pattern.
Microsoft's 1.0 announcement positions Agent Framework as production-ready for both .NET and Python with stable APIs and long-term-support commitment.

Highlights migration assistants for Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, plus MCP, upcoming A2A support, DevUI, Foundry hosting, observability, evaluations, frontend streaming adapters, skills, and agent harness support.
Useful news hook: teams on release-candidate packages can upgrade with a package bump, while SK and AutoGen users should now start migration planning.
Neutral coverage of the 1.0 release, emphasizing .NET/Python availability, stable APIs, LTS, and the successor-path narrative.
Summarizes the message that Agent Framework builds on Semantic Kernel and AutoGen rather than discarding their ideas.
Good competitor angle: make the migration article more practical than news coverage by adding inventory checklists, feature mappings, and phased rollout guidance.
Independent migration playbook aimed at .NET and Python teams moving prototypes from Semantic Kernel or AutoGen to Agent Framework 1.0.
Emphasizes approvals, background runs, production hardening, and avoiding common migration traps.
Competitive gap to exploit: go deeper on exact SK and AutoGen object mappings, migration sequencing, test strategy, and rollback paths.

stats.fact: Microsoft announced Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 for both .NET and Python in April 2026, describing it as production-ready with stable APIs and a long-term-support commitment.
The 1.0 announcement says new projects can install Agent Framework with `pip install agent-framework` for Python or `dotnet add package Microsoft.Agents.AI` for .NET.

Microsoft's 1.0 feature set includes MCP support, migration assistants for Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, DevUI, Foundry Hosted Agent integration, observability/evaluations, AG-UI/CopilotKit/ChatKit adapters, skills, and coding-agent harness integrations.

Microsoft Learn lists Semantic Kernel migration benefits as simplified API surface, better performance from optimized object creation and memory usage, a unified interface across AI providers, and improved developer experience.

The Semantic Kernel migration guide says Agent Framework Python is installed as `agent-framework`, imports from `agent_framework`, and can be reduced to provider-specific packages such as `agent-framework-foundry` when teams know exactly what they need.
The AutoGen migration guide describes Agent Framework as a multi-language SDK developed by core AutoGen and Semantic Kernel teams and designed as the new foundation for Microsoft agent applications.

Microsoft Agent Framework's GitHub README says MAF is for production-grade agents and multi-agent workflows in .NET and Python, including graph-based patterns, durability, restartability, observability, governance, and human-in-the-loop control.
As of June 2026, PyPI lists `agent-framework` 1.8.1 released on June 9, 2026, indicating active post-1.0 package iteration.
PyPI Stats reports `agent-framework` at roughly 1.14 million downloads in the last month, 267,255 in the last week, and 39,876 in the last day at the time of research.

NuGet lists Microsoft.Agents.AI 1.10.0 as updated on June 12, 2026, and the MicrosoftAgentFramework NuGet profile shows related packages such as Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows.Generators at 78,833 total downloads.

Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index says 66% of surveyed AI users report more time for high-value work, 58% report producing work they could not have produced a year earlier, and 16% of AI users are advanced 'Frontier Professionals' who use agents for multi-step workflows and multi-agent systems.

Microsoft's Agentic AI adoption maturity model advises teams to assess agent adoption across strategy, process transformation, governance, value realization, architecture, operations, organizational readiness, and responsible AI rather than only technical capability.

angles: Lead with a phased migration path: inventory existing SK/AutoGen code, migrate single-agent paths first, move tools and sessions next, then replace group chat/orchestration patterns with Agent Framework workflows.

Treat Semantic Kernel and AutoGen differently: SK users mainly unwind Kernel/plugin/thread abstractions; AutoGen users mainly map AssistantAgent/model clients/tools/group chats/checkpointing into Agent Framework equivalents.
Position Agent Framework as Microsoft's forward path, but avoid claiming old projects must rewrite immediately; critical systems need compatibility, test coverage, and rollback windows.
Use 'production hardening' as the unique value: sessions, checkpointing, observability, human-in-the-loop, Foundry hosting, MCP, A2A, and governance matter more than a simple import rename.
Add a migration risk matrix covering tool schema drift, conversation state, streaming behavior, hosted thread cleanup, provider-specific options, async patterns, and evaluation baseline changes.
Give both .NET and Python readers parallel examples or checklists, because Agent Framework 1.0 is cross-language but migration surfaces differ by ecosystem.
Differentiate stable core from fast-moving integrations: PyPI/NuGet versions are already beyond 1.0, so writers should tell teams to pin versions, read release notes, and isolate preview features.
Connect migration to agent maturity: moving frameworks is only useful if teams also add evals, tracing, approval gates, security review, and operational ownership.
